title: The wise woman of Abel (2 Samuel 20:14–22)
hook: a woman on the wall saves her town with a few wise words
carry: one wise voice saves a city

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cry from the room over the gate: my son, my son. Your line was would I had died for thee. Today the kingdom is still cracking, and one voice from a town wall saves a town.

The battering has already started. Absalom is dead, but the kingdom hasn't settled. A man named Sheba son of Bichri has blown a trumpet and shouted: we have no part in David. Joab, back at the head of David's army, has chased him to a walled town called Abel of Beth-maacah. Sheba is inside. The army has thrown up a siege mound against the town, and the soldiers are battering the wall. Everyone inside is about to pay for one man. Then, from the top of the wall, a woman calls out.
screen: `WE HAVE NO PART IN DAVID.` → `A SIEGE AT ABEL.` → `A VOICE FROM THE WALL.`

segments.voice: The text calls her a wise woman, and never gives her name. Her first words: hear, hear! Tell Joab to come near, so I can speak with him. And Joab comes. She doesn't scream at the army or hide in a cellar. She asks for a conversation with the one person who can stop it. Are you Joab? I am. Then listen to the words of your handmaid. I'm listening. And she makes her case. First, the town's name: in the old days people said, ask counsel at Abel, and so they settled things. Second, who she is: one of the peaceable and faithful in Israel. Third, what Joab is about to do: you seek to destroy a city and "a mother in Israel". Why would you swallow up the inheritance of the Lord? Joab answers fast. Far be it from me! One man, Sheba, has lifted his hand against the king. Hand him over, and I'll leave. She says: his head will be thrown to you over the wall. Then she goes to all the people, the text says, in her wisdom. They do it. Joab blows the trumpet, and the army goes home. It's a grim ending, and the text doesn't soften it. But a whole town was about to fall for one man's rebellion. She found out what the commander actually wanted, named what was at stake, and found the narrow way through. The text records no other voice from that wall. Hers was enough.
screen: `HEAR, HEAR! TELL JOAB TO COME NEAR.` · `ASK COUNSEL AT ABEL.` · then, large: `A MOTHER IN ISRAEL.` · then: `ONE MAN, NOT THE CITY.` · `ONE WISE VOICE SAVES A CITY.`

segments.voice: Think of a place where something is heading toward damage: a group chat turning cruel, a decision no one is questioning. Ask the wise woman's questions: who can actually stop this, what do they really want, what's at stake that they might not see? Then shape one calm, clear sentence and just have it ready; if you pray, you can ask for wise words.
Wise woman. The unnamed woman on Abel's wall who asked for the commander and spoke for her city. Today's word.
Your line: one wise voice saves a city. And a mother in Israel was still standing. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jews read the wise woman of Abel as part of the book of Samuel; some readers set her beside the wise woman of Tekoa in chapter 14, and one midrash identifies her with Serah, the daughter of Asher.

chat.says: How did one woman on a wall stop a whole army?
options: She asked for Joab, named what was at stake, and found what he really wanted.
She threatened Joab that the town's soldiers would destroy his army.
She paid Joab a ransom of silver, so he lifted the siege and left.
chat.meaning: She called for Joab, reminded him Abel was a mother in Israel, learned he wanted only Sheba, and the siege ended.

Sheba.meaning: Sheba son of Bichri, who rose against David

notes: Verify JPS 1917 wording 'a mother in Israel' at 2 Samuel 20:19.
The dialogue (20:16–21) is paraphrased; 'ask counsel at Abel' paraphrases 20:18.
The grim ending (Sheba's head thrown over the wall, 20:22) is stated plainly without detail.
howItsDone mentions the wise woman of Tekoa (2 Samuel 14) as a parallel; Keeper may prefer to drop it.

Audit: 'she is remembered alongside other wise women' was an unsourced generalization; howItsDone now says 'some readers' and adds the midrashic identification with Serah bat Asher (Genesis Rabbah 94:9; please confirm the reference). 'Changes everything' in the review softened. 'The king's commander' changed: David had given the command to Amasa (19:14), and Joab took it back by killing him (20:10).
Editor pass: cut geography ('north') and the narrator's count ('three parts') not in the text, and the invented 'next morning'.
